summary: After praying alone through the evening, Jesus walks across the stormy sea to His disciples, lifts sinking Peter, and the wind ceases as He enters the boat.
key_insight: Jesus’ words “It is I” are, in Greek, simply “I am,” the name God gave Himself at the burning bush (Exodus 3:14). Walking on the sea, which Job says God alone does (Job 9:8), Jesus speaks God’s own name to frightened men.
story: After the feeding, Jesus immediately made His disciples get into the boat and go ahead of Him to the other side, toward Bethsaida, {Mk} while He sent the crowds away. Then He went up on the mountain by Himself to pray. When evening came, He was alone there. {Mt}

The disciples set out across the sea toward Capernaum. It was already dark, and Jesus had not come to them. {Jn} A strong wind was against them, and the boat, now in the middle of the sea, was tossed by the waves. {Mt} From the land, Jesus saw them straining at the oars. {Mk} They had rowed about three or four miles. {Jn}

About the fourth watch of the night He came to them, walking on the sea, and would have passed them by. {Mk} When the disciples saw Him, they were troubled. “It is a ghost!” they said, and they cried out for fear. {Mt} But immediately Jesus spoke to them: “Be of good cheer! It is I; do not be afraid.”

Peter answered Him, “Lord, if it is You, command me to come to You on the water.” Jesus said, “Come.” Peter climbed down out of the boat and walked on the water toward Jesus. But when he saw that the wind was boisterous, he was afraid, and beginning to sink he cried out, “Lord, save me!” Immediately Jesus stretched out His hand and caught him. “O you of little faith,” He said, “why did you doubt?” {Mt}

Then they willingly received Him into the boat, {Jn} and the wind ceased. Those in the boat worshiped Him, saying, “Truly You are the Son of God.” {Mt} Mark says they were amazed beyond measure, for they had not understood about the loaves, because their heart was hardened. {Mk} At once the boat was at the land where they were going. {Jn}
differences: Only Matthew tells of Peter walking on the water and Jesus catching him.
Matthew ends with the disciples worshiping Jesus as “the Son of God”; Mark ends with their amazement and hardened hearts.
Only Mark says Jesus saw them “straining at rowing” and “would have passed them by.”
Only John gives the distance rowed, “three or four miles,” and says the boat was immediately at the land.
Mark says Jesus sent the disciples “to the other side, to Bethsaida”; John says they “went over the sea toward Capernaum.”

fit.question: In Matthew the disciples worship Jesus and say, “Truly You are the Son of God.” In Mark they are amazed, but “their heart was hardened.” Did they understand or not?

points.label: Awe is not yet understanding
points.text: Both can be true of the same night. Frightened men can bow in awe at what they have just seen and still not grasp what it means. Mark’s point is that the loaves should already have shown them who Jesus is.

points.label: Still learning
points.text: Matthew’s confession is real but not yet full. Two chapters later Peter will confess Jesus as “the Christ, the Son of the living God” (16:16), and even then he will refuse to accept the cross (16:22).

fit.note: Worship and slow hearts often live side by side in disciples, and the two Gospels honestly show both.
fit.short: That night the disciples worshiped in awe (Matthew) yet still did not grasp what the loaves meant (Mark). Both were true.

scene.label: The fourth watch
scene.text: The Romans divided the night into four watches. The fourth ran from about 3 to 6 in the morning. The disciples had been fighting the wind for most of the night.

scene.label: Three or four miles
scene.text: The Sea of Galilee is about thirteen miles long and seven or eight miles wide. Three or four miles out, after hours at the oars, the disciples were far from any shore, “in the middle of the sea,” as Matthew and Mark say.

scene.label: Treading the waves
scene.text: In the Old Testament, only God walks on the sea. Job says He “treads on the waves of the sea” (Job 9:8), and the psalmist says, “Your way was in the sea” (Psalm 77:19).

scene.label: Passing by
scene.text: When God revealed Himself to Moses and Elijah, Scripture says He “passed before” Moses (Exodus 34:6; compare 33:22) and “passed by” Elijah (1 Kings 19:11). Mark’s “would have passed them by” probably means Jesus meant to show Himself to them, not to leave them.

witnesses.matthew: Alone tells of Peter stepping out, sinking and being caught, faith and doubt in one man. Matthew ends with the first time the disciples together worship Jesus and confess Him as “the Son of God.”
witnesses.mark: Shows Jesus watching them strain at the oars and intending to pass by, as the Lord passed by Moses. Mark is honest about the disciples: they were astonished, but their hearts were still hard, a concern that returns in 8:17.
witnesses.john: Places this sign right after the crowd tried to make Jesus king. The King they wanted on their own terms withdraws, and then comes to His own across the water saying, “It is I.” John adds the distance rowed and the sudden arrival on shore, the details of an eyewitness.

seeing.reveals: Jesus does what only God does: He walks on the sea and speaks God’s name. And He comes to His disciples in the dark, in the very storm He sent them into, having seen them straining before they ever saw Him.
seeing.living: Jesus sent them into that wind and then prayed while they rowed. Obedience can lead straight into a contrary wind. Keep rowing, and when you begin to sink, pray Peter’s short prayer, “Lord, save me!”, and take the hand Jesus holds out immediately.
seeing.ponder: In the wind you are rowing against right now, what would it mean to hear Jesus say, “It is I; do not be afraid”?

preaching.big_idea: In the dark and the wind, Jesus comes to His own and says, “It is I.”
preaching.watch_for: Matthew 14:23 and 14:24 set two scenes side by side: Jesus alone on the mountain praying, and the disciples alone on the sea struggling. The One who prays on the mountain is the One who comes across the water.
